topicName: Scrum Theory and Empirical Process Control
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Scrum Theory and Empirical Process Control"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Scrum is founded on empirical process control, or empiricism. Empiricism asserts that knowledge comes from experience and making decisions based on what is observed. In software development and complex project management, unexpected challenges frequently arise, making predictive planning unreliable. Scrum employs an iterative, incremental approach to optimize predictability and control risk."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"The Three Pillars of Scrum"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Empirical process control relies on three main pillars that uphold every implementation of Scrum: Transparency, Inspection, and Adaptation."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Transparency: Significant aspects of the process must be visible to those responsible for the outcome. This requires a common standard, shared terminology, and open communication across the team and stakeholders."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Inspection: Scrum artifacts and the progress toward agreed goals must be inspected frequently and diligently to detect undesirable variances. Inspection should not be so frequent that it gets in the way of the work."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Adaptation: If an inspector determines that one or more aspects of a process deviate outside acceptable limits, the process or the material being produced must be adjusted. An adjustment must be made as soon as possible to minimize further deviation."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Scrum Formal Events for Inspection and Adaptation"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Scrum prescribes four formal events for inspection and adaptation, as outlined in the Scrum Guide. These events are designed to enforce empirical control:"},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Sprint Planning: Inspecting the Product Backlog to select items and create a Sprint Goal."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Daily Scrum: Inspecting progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapting the Sprint Backlog as necessary for the next 24 hours."},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Sprint Review: Inspecting the outcome of the Sprint with stakeholders and determining future adaptations."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Sprint Retrospective: Inspecting how the last Sprint went with regards to individuals, interactions, processes, tools, and Definition of Done."},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Implementing Empiricism in Code and Workflows"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"In technical implementations, empirical control translates to continuous integration, automated feedback loops, and short delivery cycles. Below is an example of a configuration script that enforces continuous inspection of a codebase through automated testing:"},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"name: CI Pipeline Inspection
on: [push]
jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: '18'
      - name: Install Dependencies
        run: npm install
      - name: Run Empirical Verification Tests
        run: npm test"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"By utilizing automated pipelines like the one above, engineering teams maintain high transparency and frequent inspection of code quality, allowing them to adapt quickly when defects are discovered."}]
